ex: The brain has billions of tiny neurons.
Each neuron sends signals to other cells in the body.
In biology class, we looked at a neuron under a microscope.
Some diseases damage the neurons in the brain.
The old door has beautiful carved ornaments.
The plates have a simple blue ornament around the edge.
Modern buildings usually have very little ornament.
The artist painted a gold ornament around the frame.
ornament.note: Most often "ornament" means a small decoration: "We hung ornaments on the Christmas tree."

ex: I eat a bagel with cream cheese for breakfast.
This bakery makes fresh bagels every morning.
Can I get a toasted bagel with butter, please?
Let's buy some coffee and bagels before work.

arsenal.note: Also used for a set of skills or tools: "She has a big arsenal of recipes."

sedan.note: American English; in British English it is a "saloon".

blend.note: Most often a verb: "Blend the fruit and milk" means mix them well.

ex: Your idea makes sense to me.
There is no sense in waiting for the bus.
Does this sentence make sense in English?
In a sense, we are all students here.
sense.note: Most often "sense" means a feeling or ability: "a sense of humor," "a sense of smell."

ex: An electron has a negative electric charge.
Electrons move around the center of an atom.
Electricity is a flow of electrons through a wire.
An electron is much smaller than an atom.

voucher.note: In the US, "gift card" or "coupon" is often more common.

ex: Can I borrow your black marker for a minute?
Write your name on the box with a marker.
The teacher uses a red marker on the whiteboard.
This marker is almost dry, so I need a new one.
marker.note: Also often a sign that shows a place or fact: "a mile marker," "a genetic marker."

ex: He sent me a funny meme about cats.
This meme is all over the internet this week.
My friends share memes in our group chat every day.
Can you make a meme for our school page?

field goal.note: A term from American football and basketball.

ex: My sister has worked in high-tech for ten years.
Many young people want good jobs in high-tech.
High-tech is a big part of the local economy.
Salaries in high-tech are usually higher than in other fields.
high-tech.note: Usually an adjective in English: a high-tech phone. As a noun, "tech" is more common.

cookie.note: Most often "cookie" means a small sweet cake: "Can I have a chocolate cookie?"

ex: My father is a baby boomer, born in 1955.
Many baby boomers are retiring this year.
A lot of baby boomers own big houses.
This ad is for baby boomers, not teenagers.
The popular show got its own spin-off last year.
The spin-off follows a side character from the movie.
Have you watched the new spin-off of that series?
Fans did not like the new spin-off very much.

de jure.note: Formal; used mostly in law and politics. Opposite: "de facto."

ex: The coach called a time-out to talk to his players.
Each team can take two time-outs in every half.
After the time-out, our team scored three points.
I need a time-out from work for a few days.

déjà vu.note: Uncountable: say "a feeling of déjà vu," not "a déjà vu."

pro-life.note: Means against abortion; the opposite is "pro-choice."

low-cost.note: Used before a noun: a low-cost airline. "Budget" is a common synonym.

cosmos.note: Means the whole universe. For the area outside Earth, say "space": "fly into space."

ex: Mosquitoes spread malaria in many hot countries.
He got malaria during a trip to Africa.
Malaria kills many children every year.
Take these pills to protect yourself from malaria.

sulfur.note: Uncountable: some sulfur (not "a sulfur"). British spelling: "sulphur."

ex: The doctor tested the reflex in my knee.
Closing your eyes in bright light is a reflex.
Goalkeepers need very fast reflexes to stop the ball.
He caught the falling glass by reflex.
In some old religions, a fetish was a holy object.
The museum shows a wooden fetish from West Africa.
He has a real fetish for expensive sneakers.
Our boss has a fetish about clean desks.
fetish.note: Often has a sexual meaning; use carefully.

ex: You may feel some discomfort after the shot.
These new shoes cause me discomfort all day.
Tell the doctor if you feel any discomfort.
She tried to hide her discomfort during the meeting.
discomfort.note: Usually uncountable: "some discomfort," "a lot of discomfort."

ex: The maestro raised his hand, and the music began.
The orchestra watched the maestro very carefully.
He is a true maestro of Italian opera.
The maestro bowed to the audience after the concert.
A typhoon hit the coast last night.
The typhoon brought heavy rain and strong winds.
Our flights were canceled because of the typhoon.
Typhoons are common in this part of Asia.
The company runs its website on a cluster of servers.
Doctors found a cluster of flu cases at the school.
The city has a large cluster of tech companies.
Each cluster in the network has ten computers.
cluster.note: Most often a small group of things close together: "a cluster of houses."

ex: The techno artist played a long set at the club.
This techno artist makes music on old machines.
We bought tickets to see a techno artist from Berlin.
Which techno artist is playing at the festival tonight?
She won the first set six to two.
The tennis match lasted five long sets.
The band played a short set before the main show.
The DJ played a two-hour set at the club.
set.note: Most often "set" is a verb: "set the table," "set an alarm"; or "a set of keys."

ex: The police found a small caliber bullet at the scene.
What caliber is this hunting rifle?
The team needs players of a higher caliber.
This school attracts teachers of very high caliber.
A zebra has black and white stripes.
We saw a group of zebras at the zoo.
The lion is running after a young zebra.
The zebras are drinking water at the river.
She baked an apple tart for the party.
We had a lemon tart for dessert.
This bakery sells small fruit tarts every morning.
Could you cut the tart into eight pieces?
She plays softball on the school team.
We watched a softball game in the park.
Softball is a lot like baseball, but the ball is bigger.
Do you want to join our softball team this summer?
softball.note: The game is uncountable: "play softball." "A softball" is the ball.

ex: OMG, I just passed my driving test!
She texted me, "OMG, did you see that?"
OMG, this chocolate cake is really amazing.
OMG, I left my keys at home again.
OMG.note: Very informal; mostly used in texting.

ex: The designer made a bright visual for the ad.
The video has great visuals and good music.
We need a strong visual for the new poster.
The visuals in this game look really amazing.
visual.note: Most often an adjective: "visual arts," "a visual memory." As a noun, usually plural: visuals.
